decided_findings.section: Task 4, Step 2 / The one hazard outside the spec's footprint
decided_findings.contradicts: Checked every other place the document speaks about this probe. (1) The closing section 'The one hazard outside the spec's footprint' carries the SAME command as its reproduction block (line 2155) and must change identically — the fix must touch both sites or the two disagree. (2) That section's precondition block (`git diff --quiet -- web/e2e/a11y.e2e.ts`) is unaffected. (3) Task 4 Step 2's second expectation, the `assert-design-system-css: all 10 selectors present` line, is a different check and is unaffected. (4) The repo's own `web/scripts/assert-design-system-css.mjs` (lines 63-78) already writes emitted selectors in the escaped form via String.raw (`.size-\[2\.125rem\]`, `.data-pressed\:bg-warning`), so the escaped shape is the established in-repo convention and the fix moves TOWARD it, not away. No contradiction anywhere; one companion edit required (the hazard section's copy of the command).
decided_findings.spike: RAN, and the fix HELD. (a) The reviewed worktree still carries a real pre-fix build: `web/.next/static/chunks/42d2m7n8ftnh3.css`. Python byte-context around the only `137px` occurrence printed: `'ar(--spacing)}.mt-\\[137px\\]{margin-top:1'` -> the emitted selector is `.mt-\[137px\]`, CSS-escaped. (b) Premise confirmed: `grep -n '@source' web/app/globals.css` lists `../scripts/**` at line 35 and NO `../e2e/**` line, so that chunk is genuinely the un-excluded state the probe is meant to detect. (c) The plan's exact command against that real file: `grep -rl 'mt-\[137px\]' .../web/.next/static/ --include='*.css'` -> NO OUTPUT, exit 1, so the `|| echo` branch fires and prints 'excluded - web/e2e is no longer scanned' over a stylesheet that DOES contain the utility. The proposed `grep -rlF` form printed `.../chunks/42d2m7n8ftnh3.css`, exit 0. (d) Two engines agree, so it is not a ugrep quirk: this Mac's `grep` is ugrep 7.8.4, and BSD `/usr/bin/grep` gave BRE exit=1 / -F exit=0 on the same file. (e) Discrimination matrix on a synthetic pre/post pair (pre-fix CSS = `.mb-2{...}.mt-\[137px\]{margin-top:137px}.p-4{...}`, post-fix CSS = the same without it): pre-fix BRE exit=1 / -F exit=0; post-fix BRE exit=1 / -F exit=1. So the current form returns 'excluded' in BOTH states (it can never fail) while the -F form distinguishes them.
decided_findings.scenario: You are about to add a third test file whose comments quote design-system class names. The plan first has you add one line to a stylesheet so the CSS build stops scanning that folder, then run a probe to prove the line worked: plant a made-up class name in a comment, rebuild, and search the built stylesheet for it. The probe prints 'excluded - web/e2e is no longer scanned', so you tick the box. It would have printed exactly that before you added the line, and it prints it against a stylesheet that visibly contains the class. You have just signed off on a guard nobody checked, and the thing that guard protects is the reason this app once served every screen unstyled in production.
decided_findings.whats_wrong: Task 4 Step 2's probe searches the built stylesheet for `mt-[137px]`, but the build emits that selector CSS-escaped, as `.mt-\[137px\]`. In grep's default basic-regular-expression mode `\[` and `\]` mean a literal `[` and `]`, so the pattern only matches the UNESCAPED text, which never appears in a stylesheet. The search therefore cannot match in either state, the `|| echo` branch always fires, and the step reports success whether or not the fix landed. The closing section 'The one hazard outside the spec's footprint' carries the same command (line 2155) with the same defect, where it is presented as the measurement that justifies the change.

decided_findings.proposed_fix: Add `-F` (fixed-string matching) to both copies of the probe command - the one in Task 4 Step 2 and the identical one in the closing hazard section - so the search matches the escaped `.mt-\[137px\]` the build actually emits. Then give Task 4 Step 2 a positive control: run the probe once before the exclusion line is added, expecting the chunk path to print, and again after, expecting no output. A single `||` branch that fires either way is not a check.
decided_findings.why_it_works: Measured, not reasoned. The real built chunk in the reviewed worktree contains `.mt-\[137px\]`; the plan's command returns exit 1 against it on two independent grep engines, while the `-F` form returns exit 0 and prints the path. On a synthetic pre/post pair the current form gave exit 1 in BOTH states while the `-F` form gave exit 0 then exit 1 - so `-F` is the difference between a command that can never fail and one that discriminates. The two-run positive control matters independently of the escaping: it is what proves the search is capable of a hit at all, which is exactly the property the single `||` form throws away. The escaped form is also already the repo's own convention - `web/scripts/assert-design-system-css.mjs` writes `String.raw` selectors such as `.size-\[2\.125rem\]`.

decided_findings.title: Rail and footer surface assertions pass on a transparent surface
decided_findings.contradicts: This is the high-risk one, so I settled it against the CURRENT text rather than the lap-1 title. It is a GENUINE RESIDUAL, not a re-file. Lap 1's applied fix changed the helper's comparison from `el.parentElement` to `document.body` (line 1038 now reads `return own !== globalThis.getComputedStyle(document.body).backgroundColor;`). That fix closed the case where the assertion could never fail at all. It did NOT close the case where the ELEMENT goes transparent: `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)` still differs from body's opaque white, so the assertion still passes. The two blind spots are mirror images, and lap 1 fixed only one side - the helper's own comment even states the principle ('Against a transparent parent EVERY opaque colour differs ... so the assertion could never fail') without applying it to the element. CONTRADICTIONS THE FIX CREATES, both requiring companion edits: (1) Task 5's Interfaces bullet says Task 7's 'engine panel also has to rule out fully transparent, so neither fits this shape' - adding the clause here makes that stated reason false and it must be reworded (the real remaining reason is that the engine panel compares against an expected TINT, not the page background). (2) Task 7 Step 2's comment says 'Not surfaceDiffersFromPageBackground: this one also has to rule out fully transparent, which "differs from the parent" does not' - same problem, AND that sentence is ALREADY stale after lap 1, because the helper no longer differs from the parent at all. (3) The helper's own doc-comment warns against hard-coded colour strings; a hard-coded `'rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)'` is in mild tension with its spirit, but the plan already hard-codes that exact string in Task 7's poll, states it as measured fact in Task 6's comment, and anchors Task 8's guard on it - so the string is established in-document and no real contradiction exists. (4) Task 8's guard anchor for this assertion is `/\(page, 'player-rail'\)/`, which the fix does not disturb.
decided_findings.spike:
RAN in a real browser, and the fix HELD. Launched Chromium via the repo's own Playwright 1.61.1 against a page reproducing the exact structure and the real tokens read out of client/src/styles.css (`--background: oklch(100% 0 0deg)` at :134, `--rail: #f4f6f9` at :171, `body { @apply bg-background }` at :275-276). Measured `body` = `oklch(1 0 0)` and the rail's real parent (`.nh-drop-zone`, no background rule) = `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)`, both exactly as the document claims. Results for the plan's helper as written vs the proposed two-clause form:
  rail with bg-rail (healthy)         computed rgb(244, 246, 249)  plan=true  fixed=true
  rail swapped to bg-background       computed oklch(1 0 0)        plan=FALSE fixed=false   <- the only branch Step 5 exercises
  rail unstyled (rule never emitted)  computed rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)    plan=TRUE  fixed=FALSE  <- the bug, and the fix catches it
So the plan's helper returns true - assertion passes - for a rail that paints nothing at all, which is precisely the NH-315 failure shape (class present in the markup, utility missing from the emitted stylesheet). The proposed clause returns false there and still returns true for the healthy rail, so it adds the catch without breaking the good case.
decided_findings.scenario: You are looking at the screenshot of the player: a grey strip of buttons down the left, a grey transport bar along the bottom. Those greys are so close to the page's white that the picture comparison cannot see them go missing, so the plan adds a check beside the picture to prove the strip still has a background of its own. Then the design system's rail colour stops reaching this app's stylesheet - the same failure that once shipped a transparent, zero-width seek bar to production. The strip now paints nothing. The picture passes, because the step is too faint to register. And the check passes too, because 'paints nothing' is technically a different value from 'paints the page's white'. Both green, and the strip is gone. Worse: the step in the plan that is supposed to prove this check can fail only ever repaints the strip white - the one case that DOES fail - so it certifies a check that is blind to the case you actually care about.
decided_findings.whats_wrong: In Task 5 Step 3, `surfaceDiffersFromPageBackground` returns `own !== getComputedStyle(document.body).backgroundColor` and nothing else. An element whose background utility is absent computes to `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)`, which differs from body's opaque background, so the helper returns true and the assertion passes. Both surfaces this helper guards score far under the pixel comparator's cutoff (the rail 20, the transport footer 5, against 1408.6), so the screenshot cannot see it either. Task 5 Step 5, the step that exists to prove the assertion can fail, swaps the rail's colour for the page colour - opaque for opaque - which is the one branch that does trip it, so it certifies an assertion blind to the transparent case.
decided_findings.proposed_fix: Give `surfaceDiffersFromPageBackground` the transparent clause, so it returns `own !== 'rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)' && own !== getComputedStyle(document.body).backgroundColor`. Then make Task 5 Step 5 prove BOTH branches: keep the existing `bg-rail` -> `bg-background` swap, and add a second arm that deletes `bg-rail` from the element outright (and the same pair for the transport footer's `bg-panel`). Two companion edits are then mandatory, because the fix falsifies text elsewhere: reword Task 5's Interfaces bullet and Task 7 Step 2's comment, both of which currently say the engine panel does not reuse this helper BECAUSE the helper cannot rule out fully transparent.
decided_findings.why_it_works: The browser spike measured all three states directly. The unstyled rail computes to `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)`; the plan's helper returns true there (passes) and the two-clause form returns false (fails), while both still return true for the healthy rail - so the clause adds the missing catch and costs nothing. Two arms in Step 5 matter because one arm can only ever certify one clause: the swap arm proves the body comparison bites, the delete arm proves the transparency clause bites, and the plan's own line 'an assertion that cannot fail is worse than none' is the standard both arms are held to. The hard-coded `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)` is safe here despite the helper's same-serializer warning, because it is Chromium's own stable serialization of a transparent background (measured), and the plan already relies on exactly that string in three other places.

Built a throwaway Playwright 1.61.1 project with two shots and two baselines, confirmed green, then deleted one shot from the source and left BOTH baselines on disk: the run reported `1 passed` and exited 0. Planting a baseline for a shot that never existed also exited 0 with `1 passed`. No warning, no orphan report. So 'an eight-shot lane reads exactly like a nine-shot one' is measured fact on this version. (b) THE PLAN'S GUARD STAYS GREEN. Over that same reduced source, `sources.some((source) => source.includes('toHaveScreenshot('))` returned `true`. (c) THE PROPOSED ASSERTION CATCHES IT. Extracting names from the source gave `['one']` while the committed baselines gave `['one','two']`; set equality returned `false`. (d) TIGHTENING FOUND BY SPIKING. The naive extraction `toHaveScreenshot\(\s*'([^']+)'` returned TEN matches over the plan document, because Task 8's own guard line contains the text `source.includes('toHaveScreenshot(')` and the pattern then ran on into the next quoted string, capturing the junk name `')),\n    '`. Requiring the `.png` suffix - `toHaveScreenshot\('([^']+\.png)'` - returned exactly nine names whose derived filenames equal the nine `-chromium-linux.png` baselines the plan lists, symmetric difference empty. decided_findings.contradicts: The omission is real, but the reviewer's FIX would create contradictions and needs narrowing. They propose replacing the 'three homes' framing with 'four files' in the Global Constraints bullet and Task 3's guard comment. 'The container tag has three homes' is literally TRUE - the image tag mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.61.1-noble lives in exactly three places (the helper's IMAGE= line, the vr job's container:, the web job's container:), whereas pnpm-workspace.yaml pins the npm PACKAGE version, not the container tag. Rewriting it to four would make a true sentence false. Worse, 'three' appears in FIVE places, and the reviewer's fix names only two of them - it would leave the Review Focus bullet ('across its three homes after this lands'), the shipped shell-script comment ('asserts all three agree with the installed version') and Task 10's AGENTS.md rewrite ('`container:` lines agree with the installed `@playwright/test`') all still saying three: exactly the correct-one-site-leave-two failure gate (c) exists to catch. The clean fix is additive instead: keep every 'three homes' sentence, and extend the Global Constraints 'Image tag' bullet - which is the plan's own canonical statement of the bump contract - to say that a bump ALSO re-syncs pnpm-workspace.yaml's three version-exact excludes, enforced by a different job. I verified the plan currently never mentions pnpm-workspace.yaml, minimumReleaseAge, or check:supply-chain-pins anywhere, so nothing else in the document can contradict the addition.
decided_findings.spike: Verified every factual claim against the repo. `pnpm-workspace.yaml` sets `minimumReleaseAge: 10080` (7 days) and its `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` carries exactly the three version-exact entries the finding names: `playwright-core@1.61.1`, `playwright@1.61.1`, `'@playwright/test@1.61.1'`. Its own inline comment confirms the mechanism - 'minimumReleaseAgeExclude is also the CVE fast-track' and 'These pins are version-EXACT: when the lockfile bumps them the exclude stops matching and no-downgrade re-trips. `pnpm run check:supply-chain-pins` (CI lint + pre-push) fails early'. I ran the guard: `node tooling/check-supply-chain-pins.mjs` -> '✓ 6 supply-chain pins in sync with pnpm-lock.yaml'. I confirmed which jobs enforce which half by line number in .github/workflows/ci.yml: `check:supply-chain-pins` is at line 175, inside the `lint` job (starts line 112); `test:tooling` is at line 105, inside the `quality` job (starts line 83). Both exactly as the finding states. One correction: the root package.json has NO @playwright/test at all - the dep is per-package (client and web, both ^1.61.1) - so any fix text should say per-package, not root.
decided_findings.scenario: A security advisory lands against Playwright and you need the patch in today. You open this plan, because it is the document that tells you what a Playwright bump touches, and you do what it says: bump the package, update the image tag in all three places it names, regenerate the baselines. The guard the plan added goes green. You push, and the build fails in a job the plan never mentioned, pointing at a file the plan never names. The patch you need was published four days ago, and this repository refuses to install anything younger than seven days unless its exact name and version are listed in that file - which is the only reason the failure is there, and the plan gave you no thread back to it.
decided_findings.whats_wrong: Task 3 and the Global Constraints 'Image tag' bullet describe a Playwright bump as touching the container tag's three homes, and Task 3's new guard anchors those three to the installed `@playwright/test` so 'a bump is all-or-nothing'. But a bump also has to re-sync three version-exact entries in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` (`playwright-core@1.61.1`, `playwright@1.61.1`, `'@playwright/test@1.61.1'`), enforced by a different guard in a different CI job - `pnpm run check:supply-chain-pins` in `lint`, where the container half is `pnpm run test:tooling` in `quality`. The plan never mentions that file, and those excludes are also the repository's documented way to install a security patch published inside the 7-day hold.
decided_findings.before:
- **Image tag:** `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.61.1-noble`, pinned in lockstep with
  `@playwright/test` (v1.61.1 today). Baselines are regenerated on the bump.
decided_findings.after:
- **Image tag:** `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.61.1-noble`, pinned in lockstep with
  `@playwright/test` (v1.61.1 today, per-package in `client/` and `web/`). Baselines are regenerated
  on the bump. A bump also re-syncs `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s three version-exact
  `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` entries (`playwright-core@`, `playwright@`, `'@playwright/test@'`):
  the container half is enforced by `pnpm run test:tooling` in the `quality` job, that half by
  `pnpm run check:supply-chain-pins` in `lint`. A patch published inside the 7-day
  `minimumReleaseAge` window will not install at all until its exact `name@version` is in that list.
decided_findings.proposed_fix: Extend the Global Constraints 'Image tag' bullet - the plan's canonical statement of the bump contract - so it records the second half of the coupling: pnpm-workspace.yaml's three version-exact minimumReleaseAgeExclude entries, which guard enforces them (check:supply-chain-pins in the lint job, versus test:tooling in quality for the container half), and that a patch published inside the 7-day window needs its exact name@version added there before it will install. Leave every 'three homes' sentence alone - the container tag really does have three homes - and fix 'in lockstep with @playwright/test' to say the dep is per-package, since the root has none.
decided_findings.why_it_works: It adds the missing half where a person planning a bump will actually read it, without falsifying anything. The numbers and the job mapping are verified, not reasoned: the three excludes are in pnpm-workspace.yaml, the guard reports six pins in sync, check:supply-chain-pins sits in the lint job at ci.yml:175 while test:tooling sits in quality at ci.yml:105, and the workspace file's own comment already calls those excludes the CVE fast-track. Keeping 'three homes' intact also avoids leaving three other sites in the plan saying something the edit had just contradicted.

decided_findings.severity_rationale: P2 is right: the plan teaches a bump procedure that is half the work, and the missing half is precisely the half a security patch needs - so the cost falls on the most time-pressured case.
decided_findings.why_it_matters_as_filed: The next person bumping Playwright - including anyone fast-tracking a security patch - follows this plan, satisfies its new all-or-nothing guard, and still lands a red `lint` job with no breadcrumb back here. The plan counts three homes for the version (`tooling/docker-playwright.sh` and the two `container:` lines), but `pnpm-workspace.yaml` carries three more, version-exact: `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` lists `playwright-core@1.61.1`, `playwright@1.61.1` and `'@playwright/test@1.61.1'`, and `tooling/check-supply-chain-pins.mjs` fails when any of them stops resolving in `pnpm-lock.yaml`. So a bump is six strings in three files, enforced by two different CI jobs - `test:tooling` in `quality` for the container half, `check:supply-chain-pins` in `lint` for the pnpm half - and the plan names only one half. Those excludes are the repo's documented CVE fast-track (the only way to install a Playwright patch published inside the 7-day `minimumReleaseAge` window), so the missing half is exactly the half a security patch needs.
decided_findings.suggested_fix_as_filed: Replace the "three homes" framing with four files, in both the Global Constraints "Image tag" bullet and Task 3's guard comment: `tooling/docker-playwright.sh`, the `vr` job's `container:`, the `web` job's `container:`, and `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s `minimumReleaseAgeExclude` (three version-exact entries - `playwright-core@1.61.1`, `playwright@1.61.1`, `'@playwright/test@1.61.1'`). State that a Playwright bump re-syncs all six strings plus both packages' baselines, that the pnpm-workspace half is enforced by `pnpm run check:supply-chain-pins` in the `lint` job while the container half is enforced by `pnpm run test:tooling` in `quality`, and that a patch published inside the 7-day `minimumReleaseAge` window needs its exact `name@version` added to that exclude list before it will install at all.

decided_findings.title: One-build option never weighed in the builds-per-CI-run argument
decided_findings.contradicts: No contradiction - the plan already contains the rejection reason elsewhere and the addition would agree with it. Task 1's webServer config comment says 'NEXT_PUBLIC_* is inlined at BUILD time, which is why the command above runs `pnpm build` under this env rather than only `pnpm start`', and Task 9 Step 10's fallback list already frames a separate web-vr job as 'takes `web` back to three builds per CI run' - so builds-per-run is the plan's own axis and a new sentence on it fits. I checked every other builds-per-CI-run statement in the plan and none claims the three options are exhaustive, so the addition corrects no second site.
decided_findings.spike: Verified all three rejection reasons against the real CI file, and found a fourth the reviewer did not name. In .github/workflows/ci.yml the `build` job (line 180) is `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` with `uses: ./.github/actions/setup-js` and `run: pnpm run build`, while the new `web` job runs `container: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.61.1-noble` - different images, as claimed. The `build` job sets no NEXT_PUBLIC_ALPHATAB_LOG_LEVEL, so its output is not the build this lane wants, as claimed. And the fourth: the `build` job uploads NOTHING - there is no actions/upload-artifact step in it at all, so there is no `.next` artifact in existence to reuse. Taking the one-build route would first have to add an upload/download pair. That strengthens the rejection the sentence records.
decided_findings.scenario: You are reviewing this work after it lands. The case for moving the browser tests into a container rests entirely on how many times the app gets built per CI run: twice today, three times under two of the alternatives, twice if you move the lane. You read it and think of the option nobody listed - the app is already built by another job, so why build it again at all? Nothing in the plan says. The comparison looks complete but is not, so you reopen a question that was in fact already settled, and the person who settled it has to reconstruct why from memory.
decided_findings.whats_wrong: Task 9's opening paragraph argues the decision purely on builds per CI run and weighs three options - bolting a step onto `vr`, a separate `web-vr` job, and moving the lane - but never names the fourth: reusing the `.next` output the `build` job already produces and running only `pnpm start` in this lane's webServer. That is the only option that would reach one build per run, and it is rejected for reasons this plan already states elsewhere, so a reader takes the three-option comparison as exhaustive.

decided_findings.title: Dismissed engine-error leaves a fourth, unshot notation-surface state
decided_findings.severity_correction: verify-A lowered it: the only action it implies is a tenth shot, which collides with the locked 'nine shots is settled' constraint in three places, and the finding never scores the state against the 1408.6 cutoff that constraint demands. Reframed to a documentation note in Task 7.
decided_findings.section: Task 7: The two states that never finish loading
decided_findings.contradicts: The finding's FACTS are accurate and I verified all of them in the app source, but the action it implies collides head-on with a locked constraint, so the fix must be reframed. VERIFIED: the Dismiss button sets `dismissed` (web/app/play/NotationSurface.tsx:90, :223) while `failure` stays truthy, so the banner unmounts and nothing replaces it; the loading placeholder is gated `{!failure && !rendered ? <Skeleton .../> : null}` at :250, so it stays down in this state too - the area really is blank, with no error copy and no placeholder; and `grep -ni 'dismiss'` over the plan returns NOTHING, so the plan never mentions the button at all. COLLISION: the finding has no `suggested_fix` field, and the only action it implies - a tenth screenshot - runs into Global Constraints ('Nine shots. ... A tenth must justify itself; if its stated coverage IS a surface step, score that step against the 1408.6 per-pixel cutoff before writing it'), Task 4 Step 3's code comment ('Nine shots, and the count is deliberate ... A tenth should have to justify itself' / 'TWO THINGS TO KNOW BEFORE ADDING A TENTH SHOT'), and Task 6 Step 3's 'Desktop web is the v0 target and nine shots is settled'. The constraint does not forbid a tenth - it names the bar - and this finding does not clear it: it never scores the state's coverage against 1408.6, and its own stated coverage ('a stray background tint') is exactly the surface-step case the constraint singles out. So the non-contradicting resolution is a documentation note, not a tenth shot, and the human should be told that plainly.
decided_findings.spike:
RAN what could be run; the fix itself is (untested) because there is nothing to execute. Source verification: `grep -n 'dismissed' web/app/play/NotationSurface.tsx` -> `:89` (comment), `:90` (`const [dismissed, setDismissed] = useState(false);`), `:223` (`{failure && !dismissed ? (`). The banner is the `

` at :225 and the component's own comment at :232-234 states it outright: 'Dismiss only HIDES this message - it does not fix the engine, which stays dead behind it.' The placeholder's gate at :250 is `{!failure && !rendered ? (`, so with `failure` truthy it never renders - confirming 'no skeleton'. `grep -ni 'dismiss'` over the plan document returned no matches. The transport's `disabled` is a prop (web/app/play/TransportRow.tsx:32, :129-156) and the plan itself states Play never enables in this state (Task 7's opening), so 'a permanently disabled transport underneath' is consistent. No shot in the plan clicks Dismiss, so the state is genuinely unreached by all nine.
decided_findings.scenario: The player fails to start its music engine and puts up a red panel saying so, with an X to close it. You click the X. The engine is still dead - the X only hides the sentence - and what you are left with is an empty notation area: no music, no loading placeholder, no explanation of any kind, and a row of transport buttons underneath that will never turn on. It looks less like an error and more like the app forgot to load. The plan photographs the panel, and never this. So if a stray tint or a leftover overlay ever appeared in that empty area, nothing here would catch it.
decided_findings.whats_wrong: Task 7 photographs the engine-failure panel but does not acknowledge that its own Dismiss button unmounts the banner while leaving the failure in place (web/app/play/NotationSurface.tsx:90, :223). Because the placeholder is gated on `!failure` (:250), nothing takes the banner's place, so there is a fourth notation-surface appearance - blank area, dead transport - that none of the nine shots reaches. The plan never mentions the button, so a reader cannot tell whether the state was considered and declined or simply missed.
decided_findings.proposed_fix: Do not add a tenth screenshot. Add a note to Task 7 Step 2 recording the fourth state, why it exists (Dismiss hides the banner but not the failure, and the placeholder is gated on there being no failure), and why it is not shot - so a reader can see it was considered rather than missed. If the human would rather cover it, the document's own bar applies first: score the state's surface coverage against the 1408.6 cutoff, as Global Constraints require of any tenth shot.
decided_findings.why_it_works: It resolves the real gap - the plan is silent about a reachable appearance - without touching the shot count, which three separate places in this document treat as settled. The note is also load-bearing for the next person: the reason the area stays blank is non-obvious (the placeholder is suppressed by the failure, not by the banner), and it is written in the source but nowhere in the plan. Verified in the source, so the note states measured behaviour, not a guess. The scoring route stays open if the human wants the shot, and naming it keeps the decision with them rather than with the reviewer.

decided_findings.title: web job guard omits the install step's lockfile and script flags
decided_findings.severity_correction: verify-B lowered it to match the reviewer's own advisory framing and 50 confidence: the sibling `vr` job runs the same unguarded install line today.
decided_findings.section: Task 9: Move `web/`'s whole browser lane into the container
decided_findings.contradicts: No contradiction. The guard's own comment states the contract the new assertion belongs to - 'Everything pinned here is something whose loss would be SILENT' - and losing either install flag is silent, so the addition extends the stated rule rather than cutting across it. Two gate-(c) notes. (1) The plan's two headline counts for this step already disagree with each other today: Task 9's Files bullet says 'rewrite two assertions, add two' while Step 7's heading says 'Rewrite the two broken guard assertions and add three' (lap 1 raised the heading and left the bullet behind). The fix adds one `assert` INSIDE the existing test rather than a new `test()`, so it need not move either number - but whoever applies it should not treat either as a reliable anchor, and the pre-existing disagreement is worth a separate ticket. (2) Task 3's shell helper runs the same `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` line and is not guarded either; this fix deliberately covers only the CI job, which is consistent with the guard file's scope (it reads workflows and package.json, not shell scripts).
decided_findings.spike: Ran the proposed regex against the real workflow. A node script sliced .github/workflows/ci.yml the same way the guard does (`ci.split(/^  vr:$/m)[1].split(/^  [a-z][a-z0-9-]*:$/m)[0]`) and tested `/^\s+run: corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts$/m` against the existing `vr` job's block - result: true, matching the literal line '        run: corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts'. Since Task 9 Step 1 writes the new `web` job with that byte-identical install line, the assertion will match as written and fail if either flag is dropped. I also confirmed the mitigations the finding credits are real: pnpm-workspace.yaml sets minimumReleaseAge 10080, trustPolicy no-downgrade and blockExoticSubdeps true.
decided_findings.scenario: Months from now someone is fighting a stuck CI install and deletes a flag from the new job's install line to get it moving. Everything stays green, so the change ships. From then on that job quietly stops installing the exact versions the repository recorded and resolves fresh ones from the registry each run - while the browser it compares screenshots with stays frozen at the pinned image. The two halves of the renderer drift apart with nothing to say so, and the same edit also lets package install scripts run in CI again. Every other thing in that job whose loss would be silent has a check; this line does not.
decided_findings.whats_wrong: Task 9 Step 7's guard over the new `web` CI job checks the run line, the single invocation, the container pin, the absence of a browser-install step, the report upload and the job's presence in `ci-green` - but not its install line. The job's `run: corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` can lose `--frozen-lockfile` (letting the container resolve fresh registry versions while the pinned image stays put) or `--ignore-scripts` (letting dependency lifecycle scripts run in CI) with CI still green, which is exactly the class the guard's own comment says it covers.
decided_findings.proposed_fix: Add one anchored assertion to the `web` job guard in Task 9 Step 7, next to the container-pin check, asserting the install line matches `run: corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` exactly - in the same `run:`-anchored idiom the surrounding assertions already use - with a short comment saying why losing either flag is silent.
decided_findings.why_it_works: It closes the one silent-loss path the guard's own stated contract covers but does not check, using an idiom the file already uses. And it is proven to work rather than assumed: I ran that exact regex against the existing `vr` job's slice in the real ci.yml and it matched the live install line, which is byte-identical to the one Task 9 Step 1 writes for the new job - so the assertion passes on the intended workflow and fails the moment either flag is removed.

Spot by spot: 'the root dep' is ALREADY wrong before NH-320 - the root package.json has no @playwright/test at all (verified), the dep is per-package (client and web, both ^1.61.1). The vr job's container tag survives unchanged. The e2e job's Chromium install survives but narrows: the real e2e job has two install steps today, 'Install Playwright Chromium (client)' and 'Install Playwright Chromium (web)', and Task 9 Step 2's diff deletes only the (web) one. NH-320 then ADDS two spots the sentence cannot know about - tooling/docker-playwright.sh's IMAGE= line and the new web job's container: line - and Task 3's new guard anchors the IMAGE line plus both container: lines to the installed version.
decided_findings.scenario: Some months from now you are the one bumping Playwright. You search the docs, find the spec that tells you the version is load-bearing in three places, and work through them. One of the three does not exist any more the way it is described, one has quietly narrowed to half of what it used to cover, and two new places the version now lives are not on the list at all. Two of those are caught by a check, so CI stops you - but the third and fourth are prose in a README and a runbook that nothing verifies, and the document you trusted is the one that sent you past them.
